source_metadata.title: Psychosocial and psychological interventions for relapse prevention in schizophrenia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
source_metadata.source_type: systematic review and frequentist network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
source_metadata.source_boundary: The ATOM set represents claims and meta-analytic results generated or reported by this systematic review; it does not promote underlying individual-trial results to primary-study evidence.

extraction_metadata.scope_note: Review-level meta-analytic findings and source-level methods/limitations are represented. Individual trial findings are not promoted to primary-study evidence.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to compare the efficacy, acceptability, and tolerability of psychosocial and psychological interventions for preventing relapse in schizophrenia.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We aimed to evaluate the efficacy, acceptability, and tolerability of psychosocial and psychological interventions for relapse prevention in schizophrenia.

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in adults with schizophrenia or related disorders, including open or masked trials, in which relapse or rehospitalization was a primary or co-primary outcome and relapse was assessed at least 12 weeks after randomization.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We included open and masked studies done in adults with schizophrenia or related disorders.

population.label: Adults with schizophrenia or related disorders in eligible randomized controlled trials
inclusion_criteria: Relapse assessed at least 12 weeks after randomization

atoms.canonical_statement: Studies were excluded when all participants were acutely ill, had a concomitant medical or psychiatric disorder, or were prodromal or at risk of psychosis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We excluded studies in which all patients were acutely ill, had a concomitant medical or psychiatric disorder, or were prodromal or “at risk of psychosis”.

population.label: Excluded trial populations
exclusion_criteria: Prodromal or at risk of psychosis

atoms.canonical_statement: The search covered EMBASE, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, BIOSIS, Cochrane Library, WHO ICTRP, and ClinicalTrials.gov through January 20, 2020, with an additional PubMed search through April 14, 2020.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We searched EMBASE, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, PubMed, BIOSIS, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform.

atoms.canonical_statement: Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by discussion or a third reviewer; Chinese-language studies were managed by designated reviewers.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: IB and either AR or HG-M independently screened the identified references.

atoms.canonical_statement: The reviewers contacted authors of studies published in the preceding 30 years for missing or additional data and ultimately incorporated unpublished data for nine studies.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: IB contacted authors of included studies published in the past 30 years with a request for missing or additional data.

atoms.canonical_statement: The primary outcome was relapse, prioritizing operationalized relapse criteria, then psychiatric hospitalization, then clinical judgment; the primary time point was up to 12 months, with additional analyses up to 6 months and beyond 12 months.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The primary outcome was relapse. In case of multiple measures reported, we gave priority to relapse defined with operationalised criteria, psychiatric hospital admissions, and clinical judgement, in this order.

outcome.definition: Operationalized relapse criteria preferred; psychiatric hospital admission second; clinical judgment third.
outcome.measurement_method: Trial-defined relapse according to prespecified hierarchy

atoms.canonical_statement: Secondary efficacy outcomes included overall, positive, negative, and depressive symptoms, quality of life, adherence, functioning, and discontinuation for inefficacy; acceptability was any-cause discontinuation and tolerability included intervention-related adverse events and mortality.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We examined overall, positive, negative, and depressive symptoms of schizophrenia; quality of life; adherence; overall functioning; and study discontinuations due to inefficacy as secondary efficacy outcomes.

atoms.canonical_statement: Random-effects pairwise and frequentist network meta-analyses were performed with netmeta in R; binary outcomes used odds ratios and continuous outcomes standardized mean differences, both with 95% confidence intervals.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We performed random-effects pairwise meta-analyses and a network meta-analysis in a frequentist framework using the package netmeta in R.

atoms.canonical_statement: Transitivity was assessed by comparing baseline severity, inpatient status, outcome-assessor masking, sex distribution, publication year, sample size, age, and study duration across intervention groups.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We also compared the distribution of key effect modifiers across studies grouped by interventions.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review assessed inconsistency with both design-by-treatment interaction and SIDE testing and used prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses to explore heterogeneity or inconsistency.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Statistical inconsistency was evaluated separating indirect from direct evidence, and then testing the agreement of these two pieces of evidence (SIDE-test).

atoms.canonical_statement: Risk of bias for relapse was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2, small-study effects were assessed with a comparison-adjusted funnel plot and Harbord test, and confidence in primary NMA estimates was evaluated with CINeMA.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Risk of bias was assessed by IB and AR using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2 for the primary outcome relapse.

atoms.canonical_statement: The supplement reports a post-hoc switch to the updated RoB 2.0 tool rather than the older risk-of-bias tool.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The updated tool RoB 2.0 was used instead of the old version of risk of bias tool.

atoms.canonical_statement: For the cluster-randomized Li 2018 trial, the authors used reported intraclass correlation coefficients where available and ICC 0.1 when an outcome-specific ICC was unavailable.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: for outcomes for which they were not given an ICC of 0.1 was used

atoms.canonical_statement: Absolute relapse event rates were derived from odds ratios using the meta-analytic treatment-as-usual event rate as the assumed control risk.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: As ACR, we used the meta-analytic point estimate of event rates in the treatment as usual (TAU) group

atoms.canonical_statement: Eighty-five studies represented by 244 full-text articles were included in qualitative synthesis; 72 studies with 10,364 participants had usable data and entered the network meta-analysis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 72 studies (involving 10 364 participants and done between 1971 and 2019) had usable data and were included in the network meta-analysis.

population.label: Studies included in the quantitative network meta-analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: The 12-month primary relapse network included 63 studies, 19 interventions, and 9,010 participants.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 63 studies with 19 interventions (n=9010 participants; figure 2) contributed to the network meta-analysis of the primary outcome relapse at the primary timepoint of 12 months.

population.label: Primary 12-month relapse NMA population across 63 randomized trials

atoms.canonical_statement: Across the NMA corpus, mean study sample size was 142, median trial duration 52 weeks, mean participant age 32.3 years, mean illness duration 7.6 years, and mean baseline PANSS 52.34; among 9,655 participants with sex reported, 40.8% were female and 59.2% male, while ethnicity was rarely reported.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Of 9655 participants with sex indicated, 3939 (40·8%) were female and 5716 (59·2%) were male.

population.label: Network meta-analysis participant characteristics

atoms.canonical_statement: Overall risk of bias was low in 1 study, moderate/some concerns in 51 studies, and high in 33 studies; no study was high risk in the randomization-process domain.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: One study had a low overall risk of bias, 51 studies had a moderate overall risk, and 33 studies had a high overall risk.

atoms.canonical_statement: No clear transitivity violation was identified, but the authors cautioned that small numbers of studies per comparison could have left undetected intransitivity.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: there might have been a certain level of intransitivity that we were not able to detect.

atoms.canonical_statement: Treatment as usual generally consisted of standard psychiatric care including maintenance antipsychotic treatment, psychiatric follow-up, and access to community-based rehabilitative activities, without an added specific psychosocial intervention.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Patients continue to receive standard psychiatric care.

exposures.details: Standard psychiatric care, generally including maintenance antipsychotic medication and routine follow-up; no additional specific psychosocial intervention.

atoms.canonical_statement: At up to 12 months, Family intervention versus treatment as usual had a network-meta-analysis odds ratio for relapse of 0.35 (95% CI 0.24–0.52); the author-calculated relapse event rate was 16% (95% CI 11–22) versus 35% for treatment as usual.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Family intervention: 0.35 (0.24–0.52)

atoms.canonical_statement: Family intervention and family psychoeducation reduced relapse at 12 months and beyond 12 months but not at 6 months; assertive community treatment showed benefit only at 6 months with a broad confidence interval.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Family interventions and family psychoeducation, which were effective at 12 months and longer, but not at 6 months.

atoms.canonical_statement: Cognitive behavioural therapy reduced relapse at 12 months, while estimates at 6 months and beyond 12 months were close to no difference versus treatment as usual.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Cognitive behavioural therapy showed virtually no difference compared with treatment as usual at 6 months and more than 12 months.

atoms.canonical_statement: Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were generally consistent with the main relapse analysis, but assertive community treatment, integrated intervention, patient psychoeducation, and rehabilitation showed more variable estimates; integrated intervention, patient psychoeducation, and rehabilitation lost clear superiority in six or more additional analyses.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: For integrated intervention, patient psychoeducation, and rehabilitation, the main analysis showed a superiority in comparison with treatment as usual, but in six or more additional analyses the confidence intervals included the possibility of no difference.

atoms.canonical_statement: For overall symptoms, most interventions outperformed controls, with exceptions including motivational interviewing, telemedicine, cognitive training, and case management; corresponding exception sets also occurred for positive and negative symptoms.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: almost all interventions were superior to control conditions with 95% CIs excluding no effect except for motivational interviewing, telemedicine, cognitive training, and case management for overall symptoms

atoms.canonical_statement: Family interventions were more effective than most other treatments for functioning, and mindfulness and cognitive behavioural therapy outperformed treatment as usual for functioning.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Family interventions were more efficacious than were most other treatments in improving functioning; mindfulness and cognitive behavioural therapy outperformed treatment as usual.

atoms.canonical_statement: Overall dropout did not differ across most interventions; integrated interventions had lower all-cause dropout than treatment as usual, and cognitive behavioural therapy had lower dropout due to inefficacy than treatment as usual.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: no differences emerged in overall dropout rates, except for a superiority of integrated interventions compared with treatment as usual

atoms.canonical_statement: Integrated interventions were associated with less non-compliance than treatment as usual, whereas relapse prevention programmes had a higher probability of non-compliance than most other treatments.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: integrated interventions were associated with less non-compliance

atoms.canonical_statement: Other adverse-event data were too sparse for analysis; death was rare and did not differ between treatments, and data were insufficient for depressive symptoms, adherence, quality of life, and suicide.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Data on other adverse events associated with psychological interventions were scarce and could not be analysed.

atoms.canonical_statement: For relapse at 12 months, the supplement classified between-study heterogeneity as low-moderate (between-study variance 0.2748) and found some evidence of inconsistency (design-by-treatment p=0.0914; 4 of 21 detachable comparisons had SIDE p<0.10).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Relapse 12 months (OR) 0.2748 ... low-moderate

atoms.canonical_statement: The small-study-effect assessment did not suggest funnel-plot asymmetry; the Harbord test was t=0.58294 with 74 degrees of freedom and p=0.5617.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Harbord test for funnel plot asymmetry ... p-value 0.5617

atoms.canonical_statement: CINeMA confidence for primary-network comparisons ranged from moderate to very low; no high-confidence estimates were reported in the article summary.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Judgements about confidence in the estimates (CINeMA) ranged from moderate to very low.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors judged the relapse-prevention evidence most robust for family interventions, family psychoeducation, and cognitive behavioural therapy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: results for family interventions, family psychoeducation and cognitive behavioural therapy were robust

atoms.canonical_statement: Many treatment comparisons were informed by only one or two studies, producing thin networks and low power to detect differences or inconsistency.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the available data for many comparisons are based on few studies (in some cases just one or two studies)

atoms.canonical_statement: Most included trials had some concerns or high risk of bias, and therapist and participant masking is not feasible for psychological interventions.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Masking of therapist and patients is not possible in studies on psychological interventions

atoms.canonical_statement: Although stringent eligibility criteria and transitivity checks were used, heterogeneity and inconsistency remained for some outcomes, and poorly defined relapse prevented the planned analysis of different relapse definitions except for hospitalization.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: there was heterogeneity and inconsistency for some outcomes.

atoms.canonical_statement: All psychosocial and psychological interventions were added to pharmacological treatment, but medication regimens and doses were rarely reported, limiting separation of psychosocial effects from pharmacotherapy and assessment of treatment-effect modification.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Details on medication received and doses are very rarely provided

atoms.canonical_statement: Patient psychoeducation, integrated interventions, and relapse prevention programmes showed substantial variability across subgroup and sensitivity analyses despite favorable primary 12-month estimates.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: there was considerable variability in different subgroup and sensitivity analyses.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors recommended that clinicians and policy makers prioritize family interventions, family psychoeducation, and cognitive behavioural therapy when allocating psychosocial resources for maintenance treatment in schizophrenia.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: policy makers and clinicians should consider giving priority to family interventions, family psychoeducation, and cognitive behavioural therapy
